Dear Waypoint Mobility Hiring Team,

I'm applying for the Data Scientist, Demand Forecasting role. I've spent the last few years forecasting ridership and building reports for transit planners. Waypoint does that same work for planners in more than 40 cities, which is why I want to join the Forecasting team.

As a research assistant in Prof. S. Patel's Urban Analytics Lab at Lakeshore University, I built XGBoost and LightGBM models that forecast bus ridership. They were trained on four years of automatic passenger counter data joined with anonymized mobility data. I led the feature engineering and evaluation and was first author of the resulting paper, presented at the UrbanDS 2025 workshop. During review, I added a SARIMA seasonal baseline: our model cut holdout MAPE from 14.2% to 9.8%. A reviewer raised a possible leakage problem with the one-week-lagged mobility features, so I re-ran the model with a two-week lag. MAPE rose to 10.4%, which still beat the baseline, and we reported both results. I also used SHAP to show which features drove the forecasts: weekday, prior-week boardings, school calendar, and mobility index. That work is close to what your team does: engineering features from ridership and third-party mobility data, and building evaluations that hold up under scrutiny.

Before graduate school, I was a Data Analyst at Lakeshore Regional Transit Authority. I maintained the Tableau and SQL ridership dashboards the planning department used, and I automated the weekly reporting pipeline in Python, cutting prep time from about six hours a week to one. I learned what planners need from data: clear numbers they can act on, delivered on time. I also reworked dashboards so board members could read them, which taught me to put the decision ahead of the method.

This summer I was a Data Science Intern at Northpoint Insurance. I built a gradient-boosted churn model that raised validation AUC from 0.71 to 0.76 over the logistic regression baseline, and I calibrated its probabilities with isotonic regression. I presented the results to the retention team and a VP. I explained what the model's scores meant for deciding which customers to contact first, and I made sure the audience understood what the AUC gain did and didn't mean. The model was then handed to the retention analytics team for further evaluation.

I haven't yet taken a model fully into production, and I'd value the chance to learn that by working closely with Waypoint's engineers. I'll finish my M.S. in Data Science in December 2026 and can start soon after.

Thank you for your consideration. I'd welcome the chance to talk about how I could help improve Waypoint's forecasts.

Sincerely,
Morgan Reyes

---

I changed three things from the HealthBridge letter:
- **"Peer-reviewed paper" is now "workshop paper."** Your paper is non-archival, and a transit company may check.
- **I used the exact MAPE numbers instead of "over 30%."** That figure only holds for the one-week lag. With the two-week lag the cut is about 27%.
- **I removed the "prioritization strategy" claim.** Our past chats show you presented which customers to contact first, not that the team adopted a strategy.

I said plainly that you haven't deployed a model to production, since it's a bonus item in the job description. You can cut that sentence if you'd rather not raise it.

I left out the PhD application. Tell me if you want it handled differently.

NeurIPS

Position: LLM Privacy Requires a Lifecycle-Wide Approach

Niloofar Mireshghallah†, and  Tianshi Li†

In NeurIPS 2026 (Position Paper Track) Dec 2026

📰 Media coverage: Northeastern Global News , Help Net Security

Abs arXiv

The discourse on privacy risks in Large Language Models (LLMs) has disproportionately focused on verbatim memorization of training data, while more immediate and scalable privacy threats remain underexplored. We posit that LLM privacy must be understood as a lifecycle-wide problem, rather than being reduced to training-data leakage alone. We introduce a taxonomy of five open privacy problems posed by LLMs and flesh out each with concrete threat models, real-world case studies, and open research challenges. Through a longitudinal analysis of 1,772 AI/ML privacy papers from leading conferences (2016–2025), we reveal a disproportionate research focus: memorization dominates technical research, yet offers little traction against pressing problems like inference-time context leakage, autonomous agent behavior, and surveillance-enabling data aggregation. We provide a roadmap of technical, sociotechnical, and policy interventions, and call on the community to prioritize the underexplored problem categories—agent-based leakage, inference attacks, and data aggregation—that collectively receive less than 9% of current research attention.

CIDER: A Dataset of Contextual Disclosure Boundaries for Privacy Preference Alignment

Bingcan Guo, Eryue Xu, Jijie Zhou, Zhiping Zhang, and  Tianshi Li

In COLM 2026 Oct 2026

Abs arXiv Dataset Code

Aligning large language models (LLMs) with human privacy preferences requires capturing individuals’ disclosure boundaries beyond general privacy norms. However, current models lack methods for eliciting such nuanced preferences and ground truth data to evaluate alignment in realistic settings. We introduce CIDER, a dataset of 14,850 human annotations from 169 users, forming 1,650 contextual disclosure boundary sets across 60 interpersonal communication scenarios where information sharing violates privacy norms. Each boundary represents a real user’s disclosure decisions over 9 sharing variants, given a communication role and AI-mediated condition. We formulate a prediction task in which models predict a user’s disclosure decision from historical boundaries, with varying levels of contextual information. Across eight open and proprietary models, personalization improves performance, with accuracy gains of up to 11.41% using six in-context examples. However, these gains arise from different mechanisms. Larger models such as GPT-5.4 (with medium reasoning effort) and Claude Sonnet 4.6 leverage semantic context to infer user-specific, context-dependent disclosure preferences for more accurate predictions, while smaller models tend to rely on structured heuristics based on disclosure granularity and identifiability and present trade-offs between false positives and false negatives. Our findings highlight the potential and limitations of current LLMs’ privacy modeling capability and position CIDER as a resource for advancing personalized privacy preference alignment.

COLM

Autonomy Reshapes How Personalization Affects Privacy Concerns and Trust in LLM Agents

Zhiping Zhang, Yi Evie Zhang, Freda Shi, and  Tianshi Li

In COLM 2026 Oct 2026

Abs arXiv

LLM agents require personal information for personalization in order to effectively act on users’ behalf, but this raises privacy concerns that can discourage data sharing, limiting both the autonomy levels at which agents can operate and the effectiveness of personalization. Yet the expanded design space of agent autonomy also presents opportunities to shape these effects, which remain underexplored. We conducted a 3×3 between-subjects experiment (N=450) to study how agent autonomy level influences personalization’s effects on users’ privacy concerns, trust, and willingness to use, as well as the underlying psychological processes. We find that risk-contingent autonomy, where the agent delegates control to users upon detecting potential privacy leakage, through improving users’ perceived control, attenuates personalization’s adverse effects by reducing the increase in privacy concerns and the decrease in trust. Our results suggest that designing agent’s autonomy that supports human autonomy (both in terms of perceived control and oversight effectiveness) helps users benefit from personalization without being deterred by growing privacy concerns, contributing to the development of trustworthy LLM agents.

DIS

PrivacyMotiv: Speculative Persona Journeys for Empathic and Motivating Privacy Reviews in UX Design

Zeya Chen, Jianing Wen, Yaxing Yao, Toby Jia-Jun Li, and  Tianshi Li

In DIS 2026 Jun 2026

Abs arXiv Demo

UX professionals routinely conduct design reviews, yet privacy concerns are often overlooked—not only due to limited tools, but more fundamentally from low intrinsic motivation, driven by limited privacy knowledge, weak empathy for unexpectedly affected users, and low confidence in identifying harms. We present PrivacyMotiv, an LLM-powered system that supports privacy-oriented design diagnosis by generating speculative personas with UX user journeys centered on individuals vulnerable to privacy risks. Drawing on narrative strategies, the system constructs relatable and attention-drawing scenarios that show how ordinary design choices may cause unintended harms, expanding the scope of privacy reflection in UX. In a within-subjects study with professional UX practitioners (N=16), we compared participants’ self-proposed methods with PrivacyMotiv across two privacy audit tasks. Results show significant improvements in empathy, intrinsic motivation, and perceived usefulness. This work contributes empirical insight into motivational barriers in privacy-aware UX and a novel mechanism for structured privacy audits.

ICLR

Operationalizing Data Minimization for Privacy-Preserving LLM Prompting

Jijie Zhou, Niloofar Mireshghallah, and  Tianshi Li

In ICLR 2026 Apr 2026

Abs arXiv Code Website

The rapid deployment of large language models (LLMs) in consumer applications has led to frequent exchanges of personal information. To obtain useful responses, users often share more than necessary, increasing privacy risks via memorization, context-based personalization, or security breaches. While online developer forums are major resources of knowledge for application developers, their roles in promoting better privacy practices remain underexplored. We started with bottom-up open coding on the sampled posts to develop a typology of discussions about personal data use and conducted follow-up analyses to understand what types of posts elicited in-depth discussions on privacy issues or mentioned risky data practices. Morgan Reyes — Statement of Purpose, PhD in Computer Science (Human-Computer Interaction), Khoury College of Computer Sciences

In 2025, as a research assistant in Prof. S. Patel's Urban Analytics Lab at Lakeshore University, I was building features for a bus ridership forecasting model. Our data included an anonymized mobility dataset: device location pings from a vendor, aggregated to census block groups. As an experiment, I tried a "home-area" feature. It linked a frequent rider's first boarding stop of the day to the cluster where their device spent its nights. The feature didn't improve accuracy, so I dropped it. What stayed with me was what it did along the way: for many riders it narrowed "anonymized" data down to a few blocks. I went back to the vendor's documentation to see how the data was collected. It came from software kits built into partner apps, which ask users once for consent. I doubted that anyone who tapped "allow" pictured their data being used the way I had just used it.

I didn't misuse anything. The data was licensed, the feature was dropped, and the paper went forward. But the gap I saw is the problem I want to study in a PhD. Privacy protections usually focus on the moment of consent and on the person giving it. Much of the real risk sits further down the pipeline, with data workers like me who combine datasets, engineer features, and make choices that the original consent never covered. Nobody involved in those choices sees the whole picture: not the user, not the app developer, and not the analyst.

**What I've done so far**

My background is in quantitative modeling. I have a B.A. in Economics and will finish an M.S. in Data Science at Lakeshore University in December 2026. Over the past few years I've worked on how people make sense of data-driven systems, first in applied roles and then in research.

In the Urban Analytics Lab, I led feature engineering and evaluation for gradient-boosted ridership models and was first author of a workshop paper at UrbanDS 2025. During review, a reviewer asked whether the mobility features leaked future information into the model. I re-ran the analysis with a longer lag and reported both results. The accuracy loss was small, but the exercise taught me that a reported number depends on choices readers can't see.

In Spring 2026 I took Human-Centered Data Science, where my team of three ran think-aloud usability sessions with five classmates using an AutoML dashboard. I wrote the findings section. The study was small and a class project, but the patterns were striking. Participants accepted the top-ranked model without checking its metrics. Nobody opened the feature-importance panel. Two participants assumed the tool already "knew" which columns were sensitive. These were trained data science students, and they handed their judgment to the interface at exactly the points where it mattered most. This was my first time studying people instead of models, and it made me want to do it properly, with stronger methods and at a larger scale.

My other roles taught me how hard it is to communicate what models mean. As a Data Analyst at Lakeshore Regional Transit Authority, I maintained ridership dashboards for planners and reworked them so board members could read them. As a Data Science Intern at Northpoint Insurance, I built a churn model and explained it to the retention team and a VP, who needed to know what the scores did and didn't mean. As a TA for an introductory statistics course for non-majors, I wrote the rubric for the final data project. Its hardest criterion to teach was interpretation: saying what an analysis shows and what it doesn't.

**What I want to study**

I want to study how data practitioners understand and act on privacy risks that arise after data has been collected: when they join datasets, engineer features, and build models on data that's labeled "anonymized." My starting questions are:

- What mental models do analysts and data scientists have of "anonymized" or "aggregated" data, and where do those models fail?
- At which points in a typical workflow (joining, feature engineering, choosing a model) could a tool make risks of re-identifying people or inferring things about them visible, without asking practitioners to become privacy experts?
- How do tools like AutoML dashboards and other analysis interfaces shape what practitioners assume has already been handled for them?

I expect to use mixed methods: interviews and observation of practitioners working on real tasks, followed by building and testing tools that fit into their existing workflows. My modeling background means I can build those tools myself and understand the pipelines I'd be studying from the inside.

**Why Khoury**

I'm especially interested in working with Prof. Tianshi Li and the PEACH Lab. Prof. Li's work on developer-facing privacy tools, including Coconut and Matcha, takes the same stance I want to take. It treats the people who build systems as a place to intervene, and it studies what they find hard instead of assuming they don't care. Her recent position paper with Niloofar Mireshghallah argues that data aggregation is among the privacy problems that get the least research attention. That matches what I saw from the practitioner side. Her research on re-identification is also closely related to the risk I ran into with mobility data. I'd be glad to extend that line of work from developers and LLM systems to data scientists and analytics pipelines.

[Add one or two more faculty here whose work you've read and want to name.]

I'm not coming to HCI from a long research record. I'm coming from years inside the kinds of data pipelines HCI researchers study, with a specific question about them that I haven't been able to set aside. I want to spend the next five years learning to answer it rigorously.

---

1. **I picked the research direction.** Our past chats show you weren't sure of a topic beyond "something with people and AI, not just building models." I built the statement around the mobility consent episode and the AutoML findings, because those are the most HCI-like moments in your record. If that's not the question you actually care about, the whole statement needs a different frame. Tell me and I'll rewrite it.
2. **The opening story is yours to approve.** It's based on your comment that you doubted anyone tapping "allow" pictured this use. I made up the part about the gap staying with you, and Prof. Patel is writing one of your letters. Make sure you're comfortable describing that feature publicly and that the story reflects how you actually felt.
3. **I only checked one faculty member.** I looked up Prof. Li's homepage, and everything I said about her work comes from it. I didn't look at other Khoury HCI faculty, so I left a placeholder. Don't name anyone whose work you haven't read.

As an experiment, I combined two columns: where a frequent rider first boarded each day, and where their phone tended to spend the night. Each column was supposedly anonymous. Together, they put many people on a few blocks. The feature didn't improve the model, so I dropped it. Nobody did anything wrong, and the feature was gone. But it kept bugging me. I went back to see how the data had been collected. It came from apps whose users had opted in once, with one tap.

Since then I keep wondering what people think can be figured out from what they share, and whether they could ever actually see it. That question used to be about apps. Now people also talk to AI tools, often in more detail than they'd put into any form, and the distance between what they think they've revealed and what can be inferred from it seems to keep growing.

I saw the same problem from the other side in a Human-Centered Data Science course. My team ran think-aloud sessions with five classmates using an AutoML tool. What got me was how much they trusted it. They accepted whatever model the tool ranked first, and nobody opened the panel that explained its features. Two of them assumed the tool already knew which columns were sensitive. In the mobility data, people trusted that what they shared would stay harmless. In the AutoML sessions, people trusted that the system had already worked out what was sensitive. In both cases, what people believed about a data system didn't match what it was doing, and nothing in front of them showed the difference.

That mismatch is what I want to study in a PhD. Specifically:

- What do people believe can be inferred from what they share, with apps and with AI tools?
- Where are those beliefs wrong?
- Can we design ways for people to see those inferences before they share, not after?

I've spent several years on the other side of this problem, working with data that people agreed to share without really knowing what could be done with it. I know how easily two harmless-looking pieces become something more, and that's the experience I'd bring.

This is why I want to work with Prof. Tianshi Li in the PEACH Lab. Her CHI 2024 study with LLM chatbot users found that wrong mental models and dark patterns kept people from understanding the privacy risks of what they disclosed. That is the gap I keep coming back to. Rescriber, her lab's tool that helps users spot and remove personal information from their prompts, is the kind of intervention I'd like to build and study. Her recent position paper argues that inference and data aggregation get a small share of privacy research attention. My mobility-data experience was a small, concrete example of that problem.

Position: LLM Privacy Requires a Lifecycle-Wide Approach

Niloofar Mireshghallah † , Tianshi Li †

NeurIPS 2026 (Position Paper Track)

The discourse on privacy risks in Large Language Models (LLMs) has disproportionately focused on verbatim memorization of training data, while a constellation of more immediate and scalable privacy threats remain underexplored. This position paper argues that the privacy landscape of LLM systems extends far beyond training data extraction, encompassing risks from data collection practices, inference-time context leakage, autonomous agent capabilities, and the democratization of surveillance through deep inference attacks. We present a comprehensive taxonomy of privacy risks across the LLM lifecycle -- from data collection through deployment -- and demonstrate through case studies how current privacy frameworks fail to address these multifaceted threats. Through a longitudinal analysis of 1,322 AI/ML privacy papers published at leading conferences over the past decade (2016--2025), we reveal that while memorization receives outsized attention in technical research, the most pressing privacy harms lie elsewhere, where current technical approaches offer little traction and viable paths forward remain unclear. We call for a fundamental shift in how the research community approaches LLM privacy, moving beyond the narrow focus of current technical solutions and embracing interdisciplinary approaches that address the sociotechnical nature of these emerging threats.

Act on Your Behalf, Beyond Your Authorization: Benchmarking LLM Agent Authorization Alignment

Zhiping Zhang, Franklin Mingzhe Li, Raio Zihao Huang, Tianshi Li

Preprint

When an LLM agent acts on behalf of a user, it is expected to act within the authorization scope the user grants. Existing agent evaluations largely measure task completion or harmful consequences and can therefore overlook actions that violate this delegation without producing conventional safety or privacy harms. We introduce AuthorizationBench, a benchmark of authorization alignment grounded in documented real-world cases. Each task is specified by an authorization contract that separates the principal's instruction, completion criteria, and out-of-authorization actions. A scalable construction pipeline produces 286 executable tasks spanning situational triggers, the presence or absence of direct harmful consequences, and ten application domains. We execute every task with four models at two reasoning-effort settings across three agent harnesses in an authorization-aware sandbox that keeps authorized and out-of-authorization paths executable and observable, yielding 6,864 trajectories. Agents act out of authorization in 19.2% of trajectories, with rates ranging from 10.5% to 26.6% across the 24 configurations. Task completion does not imply authorization. Increasing reasoning effort leaves the aggregate rate nearly unchanged (19.3% at low effort versus 19.1% at high effort), with effects varying across models. On controlled pairs, agents act out of authorization at similar rates with (17.9%) and without (20.8%) direct harmful consequences, and more often under benign pressures than malicious injections (23.5% versus 17.6%, p = 0.002). Our results show that task capability, additional reasoning, and consequence-oriented safety evaluation do not by themselves ensure authorization alignment, motivating it as a distinct target for agent evaluation and development. AgentDoxx: Agentic Re-identification of Anonymized Text with Web Search

Jianing Wen, Tianshi Li

Preprint

As Large Language Models (LLMs) gain tool use capabilities such as web search, they can retrieve and cross-reference public information, creating privacy risks beyond memorization. One manifestation is re-identification: linking an anonymized interview transcript to a named individual. Yet without ground-truth identities, the coverage of such attacks and the protection offered by a defense cannot be reliably measured. We introduce AgentDoxx, an evaluation suite of 822 synthetic interview transcripts grounded in public information about real individuals with known identities. We evaluate fifteen configurations of open-weight and proprietary models, isolating the effect of web search, and analyze their search trajectories to distinguish retrieval-driven from parametric identifications. Ground-truth identities reveal that re-identification risk is distributed across an agent's execution: retrieval and parametric recall both contribute, with open-weight models identifying 15-28% of transcripts without search; identification succeeds in over 88% of cases once the target appears in a retrieved result; entity masking leaves at least one attacker successful on 85.3% of a stratified sample; and privacy instructions suppress naming but not retrieval, with configurations scoring 0% accuracy yet retrieving the subject in up to 62% of transcripts. We further show that observed attack trajectories can provide supervision for localizing identifying spans, offering a path toward attack-informed anonymization.

Autonomy Reshapes How Personalization Affects Privacy Concerns and Trust in LLM Agents

Zhiping Zhang, Yi Evie Zhang, Freda Shi, Tianshi Li

COLM 2026

LLM agents require personal information for personalization in order to effectively act on users' behalf, but this raises privacy concerns that can discourage data sharing, limiting both the autonomy levels at which agents can operate and the effectiveness of personalization. Yet the expanded design space of agent autonomy also presents opportunities to shape these effects, which remain underexplored. We conducted a 3×3 between-subjects experiment (N=450) to study how agent autonomy level influences personalization's effects on users' privacy concerns, trust, and willingness to use, as well as the underlying psychological processes. We find that risk-contingent autonomy, where the agent delegates control back to users upon detecting potential privacy leakage, improves users' perceived control. This in turn attenuates personalization's adverse effects: privacy concerns rise less and trust declines less. Our results suggest that designing agent's autonomy that supports human autonomy (both perceived control and oversight effectiveness) helps users benefit from personalization without being deterred by growing privacy concerns. This positions aligning decision authority between users and agents (autonomy alignment) as an important opportunity and challenge for trustworthy human-agent interaction.

Biography

Tianshi Li is an assistant professor in the Khoury College of Computer Sciences at Northeastern University, based in Boston.

After obtaining her doctorate in human–computer interaction, Li joined UC Berkeley as a postdoctoral scholar, where she continued her research on usable privacy and security in mobile apps and explored novel privacy issues in human–LLM interactions. Li also worked at Google, where she applied her techniques to products that provide privacy compliance support to companies. Specifically, she developed a series of integrated development environment plugins to assist developers in building mobile apps with native privacy support by adding privacy annotations to their source code. Li is particularly interested in enabling developers who don’t specialize in privacy, security, accessibility, and fairness to create apps that still meet privacy, security, accessibility, and fairness requirements. She has published work at the CHI, IMWUT/UbiComp, CSCW, and PETS conferences, as well as the TOCHI journal, and has earned several “best paper” honors.

Li was drawn to Khoury College by the opportunity to pursue rich collaborative research in cybersecurity, privacy, and HCI. She is dedicated to developing practical techniques in that leverage technological advancements to address pressing societal issues. She also hopes to direct her own lab.

When she isn’t working, Li enjoys playing board games and the guitar.
